title: HTTP Caching Fundamentals
subtopics: Cacheability of HTTP methods and responses
learning_outcomes: Explain how http caching fundamentals affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from private and shared caches to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on http caching fundamentals in caching, conditional requests, and performance. You will connect private and shared caches to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: HTTP Caching Fundamentals matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying private and shared caches deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Caching and validators can reduce work and prevent stale reads or lost updates, but cache policy must protect sensitive representations. In this lesson, treat “HTTP Caching Fundamentals” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: HTTP Caching Fundamentals
content_blocks.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "task-v7"
Cache-Control: private, max-age=0, must-revalidate
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":"task_42","title":"Review API contract"}

# Later update: If-Match: "task-v7"
content_blocks.expected_output: An ETag identifies a representation version. A conditional write can reject stale updates rather than silently overwriting a concurrent change.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Private and shared caches”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Freshness and cache reuse” and “Caching versus application-level storage”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Measure before optimizing, and never cache sensitive data without a deliberate policy. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating http caching fundamentals. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Private and shared caches” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for HTTP Caching Fundamentals with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating http caching fundamentals as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
